title: Retention and LTV
summary: CRM, consent, lifecycle messaging, reactivation, RevShare compounding, community building and moderation, and honest LTV measurement. Retention is where paid leads keep paying you back, and it only works when every message respects the person receiving it.

lessons.title: CRM and lead data
objectives: By the end you can explain what a CRM is and which fields an affiliate operator needs.
You can map leads to lifecycle stages and calculate stage conversion rates.
You can collect and use lead data in a way that respects consent and data protection law.

steps.p: Most buyers stop thinking about a lead once the join or sign-up is counted. Retention starts by treating each lead as a person you have a relationship with, recorded in one place, with their history and their choices about contact.

d.b: A lead is a relationship, not a click
d.s: Retention starts with knowing who you have

steps.say: Let's start with a mindset shift. Most buyers stop thinking about a lead the moment the join or sign-up is counted. But retention starts when you treat each lead as a person you have a relationship with. Look at the headline: a lead is a relationship, not a click. That means one place where you keep their history and their choices about contact. Everything else in this lesson builds on that idea.

steps.p: A CRM, or customer relationship management system, is simply a structured record of every person and every interaction. It can start as a careful spreadsheet. What matters is that each person has one record that stays up to date.
d: Stage|where they are in the lifecycle
Consent|how and when they agreed to contact
steps.say: So what is a C R M? It stands for customer relationship management, and it's simply a structured record of every person and every interaction. It can start as a careful spreadsheet. Look at the cards. One record per person, never duplicated. The source, meaning which campaign brought them. Their stage in the lifecycle. Their consent, how and when they agreed to contact. And their history, messages, replies and deposits. What matters most is that each record stays up to date.

steps.p: Start with these fields and add more only when you will actually use them. Every extra field is data you must protect, so collect the minimum that lets you message people well and measure results.
steps.say: Here are the core fields. Read down the table: source or campaign, which lets you see lifetime value by source. First seen, which builds your cohorts. Stage, which picks the right message. Language, so you send the right copy. Consent, for lawful contact. And last active, which spots people who are lapsing. Start with these and add more only when you'll actually use them. Every extra field is data you must protect, so collect the minimum.

steps.p: Every lead sits in one stage at a time. Moving people forward is the job of your funnel and your messaging. Naming the stages lets you count how many people are in each and where they get stuck.
steps.say: Every lead sits in one stage at a time. Follow the flow from left to right: new lead, registered, first deposit, active, lapsed, and churned. Moving people forward is the job of your funnel and your messaging. Why name the stages at all? Because once they have names, you can count how many people are in each one, and see exactly where they get stuck.

steps.p: Example funnel for one month of Telegram traffic. Reading it as a CRM report tells you where retention work will pay most: here, many registered people never deposit, and over half of depositors are no longer active after 30 days.
steps.say: Here's an example funnel for one month of Telegram traffic. Two thousand joins, six hundred registered, one hundred and twenty first deposits, and fifty four still active after thirty days. Read it like a C R M report. Many registered people never deposit, and over half of depositors are no longer active after thirty days. Those two gaps show where retention work will pay most.

steps.p: Divide the people who reached a stage by the people in the stage before it. Track these rates weekly. A drop in one rate tells you exactly which part of the lifecycle needs attention.
steps.more: Example, from the funnel above. Registration rate: 600 ÷ 2,000 = 30%. Registration to FTD: 120 ÷ 600 = 20%. 30-day activity: 54 ÷ 120 = 45%. If next month registration to FTD drops to 12% while the others hold, the problem is between sign-up and deposit, such as a confusing verification step, not the ads.
steps.say: To find stage conversion, divide the people who reached a stage by the people in the stage before it. Using the funnel: six hundred divided by two thousand is thirty percent registration. One hundred and twenty divided by six hundred is twenty percent from registration to F T D, first time deposit. Fifty four divided by one hundred and twenty is forty five percent still active. If registration to F T D falls to twelve percent while the others hold, the problem sits between sign-up and deposit, not in the ads.

steps.p: Sending one message to everyone is easy and usually wasteful. Segmenting means grouping people by stage, language or behaviour and sending each group what it actually needs. It respects people's time and lowers opt-outs.
steps.say: Now compare two ways of messaging. On the left, the blast: the same message to everyone. Depositors get sign-up nudges they don't need, many people get the wrong language, and you see more leaves and mutes. On the right, segmenting: messages by stage, education for depositors, copy in each language, and fewer leaves with more replies. Segmenting respects people's time, and that's why it lowers opt-outs.

steps.p: These mistakes cost operators channels, bots and sometimes legal trouble. Each fix is cheap to put in place on day one and expensive to add after you have thousands of records.
d: Duplicate records|one row per person, keyed on user ID
No consent record|log how and when they opted in
Collecting ID or card data|never; KYC is the operator's job
Open sharing links|share by name, limit exports
steps.say: These are the common mistakes, each with its fix. Duplicate records, so keep one row per person, keyed on user I D. No consent record, so log how and when people opted in. Collecting I D or card data, never do it, because K Y C, know your customer, is the operator's job. Open sharing links, so share by name and limit exports. And fields nobody uses, so collect the minimum. Each fix is cheap on day one and expensive later.

steps.p: Starting rules to adapt. They turn the CRM from a record into decisions. The 30% trigger is an example; with small numbers, wait for at least a few dozen people in a stage before reading a drop.

rows: Fix that stage before changing ads
Suppress in every tool the same day
Act within the legal deadline; check it

steps.say: These starting rules turn the C R M from a record into decisions. If a stage rate falls thirty percent or more below its four week average, fix that stage before changing ads. A stop or opt-out means suppress the person in every tool the same day. No consent recorded means do not message. A deletion request means act within the legal deadline, and check what it is. The thirty percent trigger is an example, and with small numbers, wait for a few dozen people in a stage first.

steps.p: You may only message people in ways they agreed to, about what they agreed to, until they say stop. Consent is a legal requirement in many countries and it is also what keeps your channels and bots healthy over time.

d.s: Record it, respect it, honour every stop

steps.say: Here's the foundation of everything: consent first, always. You may only message people in ways they agreed to, about what they agreed to, until they say stop. Consent is a legal requirement in many countries. And it's also what keeps your channels and bots healthy over time. Record it, respect it, and honour every stop.

steps.p: Build these rules into your tools and your SOPs so they do not depend on anyone remembering. A single complaint about ignored opt-outs can cost you a channel, a bot or an ad account.
d: Record how and when each person opted in
Give a simple way to stop in every flow
Honour stop at once and permanently
Only message about what they signed up for
Never buy, sell or share lead lists
Delete data on request where the law requires
steps.say: Here are the consent rules for every operator. Record how and when each person opted in. Give a simple way to stop in every flow. Honour stop at once and permanently. Only message about what they signed up for. Never buy, sell or share lead lists. And delete data on request where the law requires. Build these into your tools so they don't depend on memory, because one complaint about ignored opt-outs can cost you a channel, a bot or an ad account.

steps.p: The safest data is data you never collected. Do not ask leads for ID documents or banking details; KYC belongs to the broker or operator, not to you. Limit who on your team can export the CRM.

d.text: Never collect ID documents, passwords or card details from leads. Restrict CRM exports to the people who truly need them.

steps.say: The safest data is data you never collected. Read the warning: never collect I D documents, passwords or card details from leads. K Y C belongs to the broker or operator, not to you. And restrict C R M exports to the people who truly need them. If you never hold sensitive data, you can never leak it.

takeaways: A CRM is one up-to-date record per person: source, stage, language, consent and history.
Stage rates show exactly where the lifecycle leaks.
Segmenting beats blasting for both results and opt-outs.
Consent and data protection law apply to every message you send.

lessons.title: Lifecycle messaging and broadcasts
objectives: By the end you can match a message goal to each lifecycle stage.
You can design a welcome drip and a broadcast that are honest and useful.
You can measure opt-outs and set a sensible sending frequency.

steps.h: The right message at the right stage
steps.p: Lifecycle messaging means each person gets the message that fits where they are. A new lead needs orientation. A depositor needs education and support. A quiet member needs a reason to come back, or the freedom to leave.

d.b: Message the stage, not the list

steps.say: Lifecycle messaging means each person gets the message that fits where they are. Look at the headline: message the stage, not the list. A new lead needs orientation. A depositor needs education and support. And a quiet member needs a reason to come back, or the freedom to leave. Each stage has one job.

steps.p: Use this table to plan your flows. Each stage has a single goal. If a message does not serve that goal, it probably belongs to another stage or should not be sent at all.

rows: How to verify, step by step
Risk basics and the platform tour

steps.say: Use this table to plan your flows. Read across each row. A new lead: set expectations, like what you'll get here. Registered: help finish sign-up, with how to verify, step by step. First deposit: onboard safely, with risk basics and a platform tour. Active: keep giving value, with weekly education. Lapsed: check in honestly. If a message doesn't serve the stage's goal, it probably belongs somewhere else, or shouldn't be sent at all.

steps.p: A drip is a series of messages sent on each person's own timeline, starting when they join. Keep it short. Four messages over a week, each with one idea and one easy next step, is a strong start.
d: Day 0: welcome and what to expect
Day 7: invite a reply or a choice
steps.say: A drip is a series of messages sent on each person's own timeline, starting when they join. Follow the flow. Day zero, welcome and what to expect. Day one, the pinned beginner guide. Day three, answer the top question. Day seven, invite a reply or a choice. Four messages over a week, each with one idea and one easy next step, is a strong start. Keep it short.

steps.p: Both have a place. Drips run automatically for each new person. Broadcasts go to a whole segment at one moment. Most operators use drips for onboarding and broadcasts for news, education and timely updates.

a.title: Drip

On the right, the broadcast is sent at one time to a chosen segment, written for the moment, and best for news and education. Most operators use drips for onboarding and broadcasts for news, education and timely updates.

steps.p: People stay where they keep learning something. Build a weekly mix from these types. Every claim must be honest, and any results you share must be real and shared with the person's consent.
steps.say: People stay where they keep learning something. Build a weekly mix from these card types. Education, one concept explained simply. How-to, platform steps with screenshots. Market notes, which give context, never guarantees. Risk reminders, regular and plain. And community voices, real ones, shared with consent. Every claim must be honest, and any results you share must be real.

steps.p: Retention built on pressure or false claims ends in complaints, bans and lost trust. These rules apply to every broadcast and every drip, whoever writes it and whatever tool sends it.

d.text: No income promises, no fake scarcity, no invented countdowns, no edited screenshots, no messages to people who opted out.

steps.say: Here are the lines you never cross. Read the warning carefully: no income promises, no fake scarcity, no invented countdowns, no edited screenshots, and no messages to people who opted out. steps.p: There is no single right frequency. Start low, watch how people react, and adjust by segment. The goal is that people are glad to see your message, not that you send as many as possible.
d: Start with about one message a day or less
Watch leaves and mutes after each send
Send less to people who never open
Respect quiet hours in each local time zone
Let people choose topics or frequency
steps.say: There's no single right frequency. Go down the checklist. Start with about one message a day or less. Watch leaves and mutes after each send. Send less to people who never open. Respect quiet hours in each local time zone. And let people choose topics or frequency. The goal is that people are glad to see your message, not that you send as many as possible.

steps.h: Measuring the cost of a send
steps.p: Every broadcast has a cost: some people leave or mute. Measure it each time. A rising unsubscribe rate is an early warning that your content or frequency is wrong for that segment.
steps.say: Every broadcast has a cost, because some people leave or mute. Here's how to measure it. Take the leaves after the send, divide by the members reached, and you get the unsubscribe rate. Measure it every time. A rising unsubscribe rate is an early warning that your content or frequency is wrong for that segment.

steps.p: Example: a broadcast reached 3,000 members and 18 left within 24 hours. Compare this with your own previous sends to the same segment, not with other people's numbers, because channels differ widely.
steps.say: Here's a worked example. A broadcast reached three thousand members and eighteen left within twenty four hours. Eighteen divided by three thousand is zero point six percent, the number you see on screen. This is an example. Compare it with your own previous sends to the same segment, not with other people's numbers, because channels differ widely.

steps.p: Run this quick check before every broadcast. It takes a minute and catches most of the mistakes that cause complaints or opt-outs, especially when several people on a team write messages.

steps.say: Run this quick check before every broadcast. Is it the right segment and language? Does it have one clear idea and next step? Is every claim true and checkable? Is there a risk reminder where the topic needs it? And does the stop option still work? It takes a minute, and it catches most of the mistakes that cause complaints, especially when several people on a team write messages.

steps.p: Most broadcast problems come from a few repeated mistakes. They are easy to spot once you know them, and fixing them usually lowers opt-outs and raises replies at the same time.
d: Same message to all|segment by stage and language
Sending too often|start at one a day or less
Hidden stop option|STOP works in every message
Never testing|send every flow to yourself first
steps.say: Here are the common broadcast mistakes and their fixes. Same message to all, so segment by stage and language. Sending too often, so start at one a day or less. A hidden stop option, so make STOP work in every message. Hype and countdowns, so send useful, honest content. And never testing, so send every flow to yourself first. Fixing these usually lowers opt-outs and raises replies at the same time.

steps.p: Starting rules to adapt. Compare each send with your own average for the same segment, not with other operators. Small segments are noisy, so judge on several sends, not one.

rows: Unsubscribe rate at or below your average
Rate up 3 sends in a row
No opens or replies for 30 days

steps.say: These are starting rules for frequency, to adapt. If the unsubscribe rate is at or below your average, keep frequency. If it's two times your average, halve frequency for that segment. If it rises three sends in a row, pause broadcasts and review content. If someone has no opens or replies for thirty days, move them to win-back, then suppress. Compare against your own average for the same segment, and judge small segments on several sends, not one.

lessons.title: Reactivation and churn
objectives: By the end you can calculate a churn rate and read a retention curve.
You can design an honest win-back sequence for lapsed people.
You can decide when to stop messaging someone.

steps.p: In every channel and every offer, many people stop engaging. That is normal. Some of them would come back with a useful, honest message at the right time. The rest deserve to be left alone. This lesson teaches both.

d.s: Some come back if you ask well; the rest you let go

steps.say: In every channel and every offer, many people stop engaging. That's normal. Look at the line under the headline: some come back if you ask well, and the rest you let go. Some quiet people would return with a useful, honest message at the right time. The others deserve to be left alone. This lesson teaches both.

steps.p: Churn rate is the share of active people who stop being active during a period. Measure it the same way every month so you can see whether your retention work is helping.
steps.say: Churn rate is the share of active people who stop being active during a period. Here's the formula: take the active people lost in the period, divide by the number active at the start, and you get your churn rate. Measure it the same way every month, so you can see whether your retention work is actually helping.

steps.p: Example: you start the month with 200 active depositors. During the month, 46 of them stop trading and do not return. Calculate the churn, then the retention, which is the opposite side of the same number.

d.text: Example: 46 ÷ 200 = 23% monthly churn, so 77% retention for the month.

steps.say: Let's work an example. You start the month with two hundred active depositors. During the month, forty six of them stop trading and don't return. Forty six divided by two hundred is twenty three percent monthly churn. And retention is the other side of the same number, so that's seventy seven percent retention for the month.

steps.p: Illustration: share of one month's depositors still active, month by month. Both cohorts lose people. The cohort with useful lifecycle messaging loses them more slowly, and that gap is where retention earns its money.
steps.say: This is an illustration of two retention curves, showing the share of one month's depositors still active, month by month. Both start at one hundred percent and both lose people. The upper line, with lifecycle messaging, falls more slowly, to thirty four percent by month six. The lower line, with no follow-up, falls to twenty three percent. That gap between the two lines is where retention earns its money.

steps.p: Before you write a win-back message, understand why people left. The reason decides the message. Asking them, in a short and optional question, is often the fastest way to find out.
d: Wrong promise|the ad did not match reality
Life changed|nothing to do with you
steps.say: Before you write a win-back message, understand why people left, because the reason decides the message. Look at the cards. Some lost money, because expectations were wrong. Some were confused, because the product felt hard. Some got too many messages, and you became noise. Some saw a wrong promise, where the ad didn't match reality. And for some, life changed, nothing to do with you. Asking them, in a short optional question, is often the fastest way to find out.

steps.p: Not every quiet person needs the same message. Split lapsed people by how long they have been quiet, and change your approach as the time grows. Days are an example; set your own by product.
steps.say: Not every quiet person needs the same message. Read down the table. Quiet for seven to fourteen days, a light, helpful nudge. Fifteen to thirty days, useful content or an update. Thirty one to ninety days, one honest, respectful check-in. Over ninety days, a clear final message, then suppress. The days are an example, so set your own by product.

steps.p: Keep win-back sequences short. Two or three messages are usually enough. The last one should make it easy to leave. After that, stop messaging people who have not responded.
steps.say: Here's a win-back sequence. Follow the flow: notice inactivity, send a helpful check-in, share a useful update or guide, send a last message with an easy opt-out, and then suppress if they stay silent. Keep it short. Two or three messages are usually enough, and after that, stop messaging people who haven't responded.

steps.p: Example. The message asks a real question, offers something useful and makes leaving easy. It does not invent urgency or dangle a bonus to pull the person back into depositing.

d.text: Hi Kwame, we have not seen you in a while. Was anything confusing on the platform?
I lost some money and stopped
That is hard, and stepping back is a sensible choice. If it helps, our risk guide covers position sizing. Or reply STOP and I will not message again.

steps.say: Here's an example of an honest check-in. In this chat, the message asks Kwame a real question: was anything confusing? He says he lost some money and stopped. Notice the reply. It says stepping back is a sensible choice, offers the risk guide on position sizing, and makes leaving easy with STOP. It doesn't invent urgency or dangle a bonus to pull him back into depositing.

steps.h: The last message: easy to leave
steps.p: Example of the final message in a win-back sequence. It offers one clear choice and honours it straight away. People who tap Stop are suppressed in every tool, and the record of their choice is kept.

messages.text: Hi Kwame, this is our last check-in. Want to keep getting the weekly guide?
Stop messages
Done. You will not get any more messages from us. Take care.

steps.say: This is an example of the final message in a win-back sequence. Look at the two buttons: keep the guide, or stop messages. Kwame taps stop, and the bot confirms he won't get any more messages. That choice is honoured straight away. People who tap stop are suppressed in every tool, and the record of their choice is kept.

steps.p: The difference is respect. Bad reactivation tries to pull people back however it can. Good reactivation offers real help and accepts no for an answer. Only the second builds a list that lasts.
steps.say: Now compare bad and good reactivation. On the left, bad reactivation: bonus bait every few days, guilt or fake urgency, ignoring past opt-outs, and messaging forever. On the right, good reactivation: real help or real news, an honest and calm tone, respect for every opt-out, and stopping after a set number. The difference is respect. Only the second builds a list that lasts.

steps.p: In gambling and trading, some people who go quiet have done so on purpose to protect themselves. Respect self-exclusion and responsible gambling tools, and never target anyone showing signs of harm.

d.text: Never message people who self-excluded, opted out or show signs of problem gambling or harmful trading. Follow the operator's responsible gambling rules and local law.

steps.say: This one matters a lot. In gambling and trading, some people who go quiet have done so on purpose to protect themselves. Read the warning: never message people who self-excluded, opted out, or show signs of problem gambling or harmful trading. Follow the operator's responsible gambling rules and local law. Respecting self-exclusion is not optional.

steps.p: Example: you send a two-message check-in to 400 people quiet for 15-30 days. 28 become active again within two weeks. Compare with a holdout group that got no message to see what the messages really added.
steps.more: Example, why a holdout? Some people come back on their own. Keep a small random group, about 10% of the segment, out of the sequence. Here 50 people were held out and 2 came back anyway, which is 4%. So the messages added about 3 points (7% − 4%), not 7. That is the true effect to judge the sequence by.
steps.say: Here's a worked example. You send a two message check-in to four hundred people quiet for fifteen to thirty days, and twenty eight become active again within two weeks. That's the seven percent on screen. But some people come back on their own. So keep a random holdout of about ten percent. Here, fifty were held out and two came back anyway, which is four percent. So the messages added about three points, not seven. That's the true effect to judge by.

steps.p: Example of how the result looks in a segment report. The holdout was chosen at random before anything was sent. The lift is the difference between the two groups, and that is the number to judge the sequence by.
steps.say: This is an example of how the result looks in a segment report. The segment has four hundred and fifty members, with a random holdout of about ten percent, chosen before anything was sent. Look at the table. The win-back group: four hundred people, twenty eight active again, seven percent. The holdout: fifty people, two active again, four percent. The lift is seven minus four, three points. That's the number to judge the sequence by.

steps.p: Agree these rules once and build them into your tools. They keep win-back work effective, legal and respectful, and they protect your channel and bot from complaints.
d: Segment lapsed people by time quiet
Send at most two or three win-back messages
steps.say: Agree these reactivation rules once and build them into your tools. Segment lapsed people by time quiet. Send at most two or three win-back messages. Always include an easy opt-out. Suppress anyone who stays silent. And measure against a holdout group. They keep win-back work effective, legal and respectful, and they protect your channel and bot from complaints.

steps.p: These mistakes waste money, annoy people and can break the law in regulated verticals. Each fix is already in this lesson; the card puts them side by side so you can check your own sequence.
d: Bonus bait|real help or real news
Ignoring why they left|ask, then match the message
steps.say: Here are the common mistakes with their fixes, side by side, so you can check your own sequence. Bonus bait, so offer real help or real news. Messaging forever, so stop after two or three messages. No holdout, so keep about ten percent unmessaged. Ignoring why they left, so ask, then match the message. Messaging the self-excluded, so suppress permanently. These mistakes waste money, annoy people, and can break the law in regulated verticals.

steps.p: Starting rules to adapt; the lift threshold is an example. With small segments, run the sequence two or three times before judging it, because a handful of people can swing the result.

A lift under one point after two runs, rewrite or stop the sequence. And self-exclusion or any sign of harm, suppress permanently. The lift threshold is an example. With small segments, run the sequence two or three times before judging it, because a handful of people can swing the result.

Match the win-back approach to how long someone has been quiet.
Keep sequences short, honest and easy to leave; then stop.

lessons.title: RevShare compounding
objectives: By the end you can calculate monthly RevShare income as cohorts stack.
You can compare the cash profile of CPA and RevShare for the same volume.
You can read RevShare terms for the risks that break the maths.

steps.p: On RevShare, every month's new depositors keep earning for you in later months. Next month's depositors add on top. Income from many cohorts stacks up, which is why RevShare can grow even when your monthly volume stays flat.

d.b: RevShare stacks cohorts on top of each other
d.s: Old depositors keep paying while new ones join

steps.say: Here's the big idea of RevShare, or revenue share. Every month's new depositors keep earning for you in later months, and next month's depositors add on top. Look at the headline: RevShare stacks cohorts on top of each other. Old depositors keep paying while new ones join. That's why RevShare income can grow even when your monthly volume stays flat.

steps.h: Commission per FTD by month of life
steps.p: Example: what one average FTD earns you on a RevShare deal in each month after depositing. It falls as people churn and activity slows. Your real curve comes from your own cohort data.
steps.say: This example table shows what one average F T D, first time deposit, earns you in each month after depositing. Month one, twelve dollars. Month two, seven dollars. Then five, four, three, three and two dollars. Look at the running total on the right: thirty six dollars by month seven. The amount falls as people churn and activity slows. Your real curve comes from your own cohort data.

steps.p: Follow one calendar month. Its income is the sum of every cohort's commission at that cohort's current age. The oldest cohort earns the least per person; the newest earns the most.
steps.say: Here's how stacking works. Follow one calendar month through the flow. Cohort one is at age three, cohort two at age two, and cohort three at age one. Add them up, and that's this month's income. In other words, each cohort pays at its own current age. The oldest cohort earns the least per person, and the newest earns the most.

steps.p: Example: you add 100 new RevShare FTDs every month, using the commission table above. In month three you have three cohorts at ages three, two and one.
steps.more: Example, the full run. M1: $1,200. M2: $1,200 + $700 = $1,900. M3: $2,400. M4: $2,400 + $400 = $2,800. M5: $2,800 + $300 = $3,100. M6: $3,100 + $300 = $3,400. M7: $3,400 + $200 = $3,600. Each month adds the newest cohort's $1,200 and every older cohort steps one age down the table. Total over seven months: $18,400.
steps.say: Let's work the example. You add one hundred new RevShare F T Ds every month, using the commission table. In month three you have three cohorts at ages three, two and one. So one hundred times five dollars, plus one hundred times seven dollars, plus one hundred times twelve dollars. That's five hundred plus seven hundred plus twelve hundred, two thousand four hundred dollars in month three. Run it on and month seven reaches three thousand six hundred dollars, with eighteen thousand four hundred dollars over seven months.

steps.p: The example as a sheet. The new cohort column is the same every month, $1,200 from 100 new FTDs. The older cohorts column grows as each earlier cohort keeps earning at a lower rate.

steps.say: Here's the example as a sheet. Look at the new cohort column. It's the same every month, twelve hundred dollars from one hundred new F T Ds. Now look at the older cohorts column. It grows each month, from zero, to seven hundred, up to two thousand four hundred dollars in month seven, because every earlier cohort keeps earning at a lower rate. The total climbs from twelve hundred to three thousand six hundred dollars.

steps.p: Illustration, in thousands of dollars per month, for 100 FTDs a month. A $25 CPA pays $2.5k every month. RevShare starts at $1.2k and climbs as cohorts stack, passing the CPA line in month four.

The flat line is a twenty five dollar C P A, cost per acquisition deal, paying two point five thousand every month. The rising line is RevShare. steps.p: Example: cost per FTD is $22, so spend is $2,200 a month in both cases. Over seven months RevShare earns more, but in month one it loses cash while CPA is already positive. RevShare needs a cash buffer.
steps.more: Example, the maths. Spend: 7 × $2,200 = $15,400. CPA: $17,500 − $15,400 = $2,100. RevShare: $18,400 − $15,400 = $3,000. Month one cash: CPA $2,500 − $2,200 = +$300; RevShare $1,200 − $2,200 = −$1,000. If you stop buying after month seven, CPA income stops too, while the seven RevShare cohorts keep earning a falling tail, as long as the program and the customers remain.
steps.say: Now the cash profile, which really matters. In this example, cost per F T D is twenty two dollars, so spend is twenty two hundred dollars a month either way. On the left, C P A: plus three hundred dollars in month one, seventeen thousand five hundred earned over seven months, two thousand one hundred profit, and it stops when spend stops. On the right, RevShare: minus one thousand dollars in month one, eighteen thousand four hundred earned, three thousand profit, and a tail that keeps paying, as long as the program and customers remain. RevShare needs a cash buffer.

steps.p: RevShare maths only works if the stream keeps flowing. Each risk below has ended affiliate income streams in the past. Read your terms and keep enough CPA or hybrid income to survive if one hits.
d: Negative carryover|player wins can cancel your earnings
Program closure|broker or operator exits a market
Tracking loss|players not attributed to you
steps.say: RevShare maths only works if the stream keeps flowing. Here are the risks. Negative carryover, where player wins can cancel your earnings. Term changes, where rates or definitions are altered. Program closure, where a broker or operator exits a market. Tracking loss, where players aren't attributed to you. And churn, where customers leave faster than planned. Each has ended income streams before, so read your terms and keep enough C P A or hybrid income to survive if one hits.

steps.p: Ask the network manager to answer each point in writing before you send volume. Vague answers on these points are a reason to choose CPA or hybrid instead.
d: How net revenue is defined and what is deducted
What happens if the program changes
steps.say: Before you send volume, read the RevShare terms for these points. How net revenue is defined, and what's deducted. Whether negative balances carry over. Whether it's lifetime or a limited period. The payment schedule and minimums. And what happens if the program changes. Ask the network manager to answer each point in writing. Vague answers are a reason to choose C P A or hybrid instead.

steps.p: If you choose RevShare, the partner matters more than the rate, because you depend on them for months. Look for licensed operators, clear net revenue definitions and a payment history you can check.

steps.p: A hybrid deal pays a smaller CPA plus a smaller RevShare. It shortens payback and keeps some of the compounding upside. It suits operators whose cash is growing but who want long-term income too.

Less risk|not all income depends on one stream

Payback is shorter, so less cash is tied up. And there's less risk, because not all income depends on one stream. It suits operators whose cash is growing but who want long-term income too.

d: Scaling on month-one data|wait for several cohort months

All income on one RevShare|keep CPA or hybrid too

steps.say: Now to measurement. L T V, lifetime value, is what a customer earns you over time. The honest way to measure it is by cohort. Take everyone who deposited in one month and track what that group has earned you, month by month. Look at the line under the headline: same start month, same clock. Measure by cohort, not by one blended number.

steps.p: For each cohort, divide the total commission it has earned so far by the number of FTDs in it. Label the result with its age, such as 90-day LTV, because the number keeps growing as the cohort ages.
steps.say: Here's the formula for L T V to date. Take the cohort's commission to date, divide by the number of F T Ds, first time deposits, in that cohort, and you get L T V to date. Always label it with its age, such as ninety day L T V, because the number keeps growing as the cohort ages.

steps.p: Example: 150 people made a first deposit in July. By the end of September, 90 days later, they have earned you $4,050 in total commission. Your cost per FTD for that month was $30.
steps.more: Example, continued. By 180 days the same cohort has earned $5,400 in total, so LTV is $5,400 ÷ 150 = $36. The LTV to CAC ratio is $36 ÷ $30 = 1.2. The cohort paid back between day 90 and day 180. Its profit so far is 150 × ($36 − $30) = $900 before overheads. Remember the lesson on overheads: if overhead per FTD is $5, true profit is only 150 × $1 = $150.

d.text: Example: $4,050 ÷ 150 = $27 LTV at 90 days. Against $30 CAC, the cohort has not yet paid back.

steps.say: Let's work the example. One hundred and fifty people made a first deposit in July. By the end of September, ninety days later, they've earned four thousand and fifty dollars in commission. Divide by one hundred and fifty, and ninety day L T V is twenty seven dollars. Cost per F T D was thirty dollars, so the cohort hasn't paid back yet. By one hundred and eighty days it earns fifty four hundred dollars, an L T V of thirty six dollars. That's nine hundred dollars profit before overheads, but with five dollars overhead per F T D, true profit is only one hundred and fifty dollars.

steps.p: The ratio compares what a customer earns with what it cost. Below 1, you have not yet earned back your cost. Always state the age with the ratio, because a 90-day ratio and a 180-day ratio are very different numbers.
steps.say: The L T V to C A C ratio compares what a customer earns with what it cost. C A C means customer acquisition cost. Here it's one point two, from thirty six dollars divided by thirty dollars, at one hundred and eighty days. This is an example. Below one, you haven't yet earned back your cost. Always state the age with the ratio, because a ninety day ratio and a one hundred and eighty day ratio are very different numbers.

Comparing cohorts at the same age

Each mistake leads to paying too much for traffic.

lessons.title: Running a safe Telegram community
objectives: By the end you can choose between a channel, a group or both, and set up roles and permissions.
You can write pinned rules, a weekly content calendar and a moderator routine.
You can apply clear moderation rules to scams, spam and complaints.

steps.h: An unmoderated group becomes a scam market
steps.p: A busy Telegram group attracts scammers within days. If nobody removes them, members lose money, complaints follow and trust in your whole funnel disappears. A community is only an asset if someone looks after it every day.

d.s: Scammers arrive as soon as people do

steps.say: Here's a hard truth. A busy Telegram group attracts scammers within days. If nobody removes them, members lose money, complaints follow, and trust in your whole funnel disappears. Look at the headline: no moderator, no community. Scammers arrive as soon as people do. A community is only an asset if someone looks after it every day.

steps.p: A channel is for one-way posts from you. A group is where members talk. Many operators run both and link them, so channel posts get comments in the group. Features change; check Telegram's current help pages.
steps.say: Channel, group, or both? On the left, a channel: only admins post, it's good for lessons and news, it needs little moderation, but members can't help each other. On the right, a group: members post and reply, it's good for questions and support, but it needs daily moderation, and scammers can reach members. Many operators run both and link them, so channel posts get comments in the group. Features change, so check Telegram's current help pages.

steps.p: Write down who holds each role before you open the group. Give each admin only the permissions they need. Fewer people with full rights means fewer ways for an account takeover to damage the group.
steps.say: Write down who holds each role before you open the group. The owner is you, with two-step verification kept on. Admins post, pin and set rules. Moderators remove spam and scams. A bot handles welcomes, filters and logs. And members ask, answer and report. Give each admin only the permissions they need, because fewer people with full rights means fewer ways for an account takeover to damage the group.

steps.p: Setting names differ between Telegram apps and versions, so look for the closest match; we are not certain these labels are current. The aim is the same everywhere: limit what new members can do until they have shown they are real.

steps.say: Let's set up the group safely. Setting names differ between Telegram apps and versions, and we're not certain these labels are current, so look for the closest match. Tap Next to follow each step. First, create the group and link it to your channel as its discussion group. Second, limit member permissions, turning off links and adding people. Third, use slow mode during spam waves or busy events. Fourth, add admins with limited rights, so moderators can delete and ban but not change group info. Fifth, pin the rules and the official admin list.

steps.p: Example calendar for a beginner trading education community. A steady rhythm gives people reasons to come back and gives moderators predictable busy times. Adjust days and times to your members' local time zone.
steps.say: Here's an example weekly calendar for a beginner trading education community. Monday at seven p m, the weekly lesson. Wednesday at seven, an open Q and A for one hour, with an admin and a moderator. Friday, a risk reminder and recap. Daily, a spam and scam check, three times. And Sunday, no posts. A steady rhythm gives people reasons to come back and gives moderators predictable busy times. Adjust to your members' local time zone.

steps.p: Example: a group of 2,000 members posts about 150 messages a day. A moderator checks three times a day, about 10 minutes each, and spends 30 minutes on the Wednesday Q&A.
steps.more: Example, the maths. Daily checks: 3 × 10 minutes = 30 minutes, so 7 × 30 = 210 minutes a week. Add the 30-minute Q&A shift: 240 minutes, or 4 hours a week. If you pay a part-time moderator $3 an hour (Example only; pay fairly for your market), that is $12 a week, about $52 a month. Compare that with one scam that robs members and gets your channel reported. As the group grows, add a second moderator in a different time zone rather than stretching one person.

d.text: Example: (3 × 10 min × 7 days) + 30 min Q&A = 4 hours of moderation a week.

steps.say: Let's work out moderator time, as an example. A group of two thousand members posts about one hundred and fifty messages a day. The moderator checks three times a day, ten minutes each, so thirty minutes a day, two hundred and ten minutes a week. Add the thirty minute Q and A, and it's four hours a week. At three dollars an hour, which is only an example, so pay fairly for your market, that's about fifty two dollars a month. As the group grows, add a second moderator in a different time zone.

steps.p: Count members who posted or reacted in the last 7 days and divide by total members. Track it weekly. A falling rate tells you the content or schedule needs work before people start leaving.
steps.more: Example: 260 active members in a group of 2,000 is 260 ÷ 2,000 = 13% weekly engagement. There is no universal good number; compare with your own past weeks. If it drops from 13% to 8% over a month while membership holds, people are drifting, and a content review is due.
steps.say: Here's a simple health number. Count members who posted or reacted in the last seven days, divide by total members, and you get weekly engagement. For example, two hundred and sixty active in a group of two thousand is thirteen percent. There's no universal good number, so compare with your own past weeks. If it drops from thirteen to eight percent while membership holds, people are drifting, and a content review is due.

steps.p: These mistakes appear in most groups that fail. Each is easy to avoid if you set things up properly before inviting anyone, rather than reacting after damage is done.
d: Everyone is an admin|give only the rights needed
Rules not pinned|pin rules and admin list
Members can post links|turn links off by default
Ignoring complaints|answer openly within a day

Rules not pinned, so pin the rules and admin list. Members can post links, so turn links off by default. Ignoring complaints, so answer openly within a day. Each is easy to avoid if you set things up before inviting anyone.

steps.h: Keep the group honest and lawful
steps.p: A community about trading or gambling is still marketing for a regulated product. Keep posts educational, never let anyone promise returns and follow the rules of the operator and your local regulator.

d.text: No posts promising returns, no signals sold as sure wins, no pressure to deposit. Remove such posts, including from members, and follow local law and platform rules.

steps.say: A community about trading or gambling is still marketing for a regulated product. Read the warning: no posts promising returns, no signals sold as sure wins, no pressure to deposit. Remove such posts, including posts from members, and follow local law and platform rules. Keep posts educational, and follow the rules of the operator and your local regulator.

steps.p: Example of the first starting rule in action. The moderator removes the impersonator, then tells the group what happened and how to spot the next one. Handling it in public teaches every member at once.

steps.p: People stay where they feel safe and keep learning. A moderated group, pinned rules, a steady calendar and honest content do more for retention than any single message. Look after the community and it looks after your LTV.

d.s: The community that lasts is the one someone looks after

steps.say: Here's the takeaway: safe, useful, steady. People stay where they feel safe and keep learning. A moderated group, pinned rules, a steady calendar and honest content do more for retention than any single message. The community that lasts is the one someone looks after. Look after it, and it looks after your L T V.

exam.q: You have 3,000 joins, 750 registrations and 60 FTDs. Registration-to-FTD fell from 15% to 8% this month while other rates held. Where do you look first?
options: The step between sign-up and first deposit
exam.why: 60 ÷ 750 = 8%. Only that stage dropped, so the problem lies between registration and deposit, such as verification or onboarding.

exam.q: A teammate wants to import a purchased list of 10,000 Telegram users into your broadcasts. What do you do?
options: Refuse: those people never consented and buying lists breaks data protection rules
Import it but add a stop option
exam.why: You may only message people who opted in to you. Bought lists have no valid consent.

exam.q: A broadcast reached 4,000 people and 60 left. Your usual rate for that segment is 0.75%. What does your starting frequency rule say?
options: 1.5% is 2× your average, so halve frequency for that segment and review content
exam.why: 60 ÷ 4,000 = 1.5%, twice the usual 0.75%, which triggers halving frequency for that segment.

exam.q: A depositor who lost money tells your bot they are stepping back. What is the right reply?
options: Offer a bonus to redeposit today
Acknowledge it, offer an optional risk guide and an easy way to stop messages
exam.why: Respectful, honest support with a clear opt-out is the only acceptable approach.

exam.q: A scammer copying your admin's name messages members asking for a "verification fee". Two members have already paid. What does your moderation rule say?
options: Remove and ban the account at once, warn the group openly and repin the official admin list
Wait to see if it happens again
Message the scammer to ask them to stop
Delete the group and start a new one
exam.why: Impersonators are removed and banned immediately, and the group is warned openly so others can spot the fake.

exam.q: Your win-back sequence reactivated 9% of a segment; a 10% holdout reactivated 6%. How do you report the result?
options: About 3 points added by the messages
exam.why: The holdout shows natural returns; the true lift is 9% − 6% = 3 points.

exam.q: Commission per FTD: M1 $15, M2 $9, M3 $6. You add 80 FTDs a month. What is income in month three?
Your cash is thin, you need payouts within weeks, and the RevShare terms include negative carryover you cannot model. Which deal fits?
options: CPA, or a hybrid with a meaningful CPA part
exam.why: Tight cash and unclear carryover risk favour fast, fixed income.

exam.q: Better onboarding lifts commission from month two onward by 25%. Base per-FTD values: M1 $12, months 2-7 total $24. What is the new 7-month value?
Your report shows one blended LTV of $40 across all cohorts, and you want to raise the target CPA to $38. What do you check first?
options: Cohort LTV at the same age, using paid earnings, and overheads per FTD
exam.why: Blended LTVs mix old tails with new cohorts and can overstate value; check same-age cohorts and overheads first.
